title: Add `SIZE_MAXIMIZE` size flag
body:
* Follow up to #116640 

Currently, custom maximum sizes serve only as a limit, reducing their usability a bit. 
The biggest remaining problem, in my opinion, is cases where I want the parent container to act as if the child were maximized at all times, even if it isn't. 

This PR resolves the issue by introducing a new size flag, `SIZE_MAXIMIZE`. This flag makes the parent container use the child's `custom_maximum_size` instead of its computed minimum size when calculating its own minimum size. For layout-type containers that support the `stretch_ratio` size flag, children with the `SIZE_MAXIMIZE` flag are prioritized during child expansion, while still respecting relative stretch ratios for maximized children. 

One good example is `CenterContainer`, which uses the child's minimum size to compute its own minimum size, so as the child grows, so does the `CenterContainer`. In doing so, however, the `CenterContainer` 's position will change, causing the child to move. Not staying "centered". Currently, the only way to avoid this movement is to set the `CenterContainer` 's `custom_minimum_size` to the child's maximum size or greater. With this new flag, the `CenterContainer` will always have a size equal to or greater than the child's maximum size, ensuring no movement and no need to modify the parent to accommodate the child, which can be really nice with dynamic layouts and deep trees. 

A second case where this is strongly relevant is with layout-type containers, like `BoxContainer`, where you want to ensure the parent container always has enough space for the child's maximum size. Currently, you need to manually compute the minimum size required to fit all the children at their maximum size (and don't forget to use minimum sizes for the others, and separations!). With this flag, the layout-type container will automatically try to provide enough room for the maximum-sized children, and will even prioritize them during child expansion. This does not necessarily mean they will have a final size equal to their maximum size, but it will prioritize them. The alternative, namely giving them all a minimum size equal to their maximum, would just brute-force their sizes. Combined with a maximum-sized layout container that thus clips its children, it just doesn't work. 

Note: 
The PR also adds centralized minimum-size logic directly to the `Container` class for "basic" single-child containers, which they can use and augment (for example, adding margins to `MarginContainer`).
